flashcards.q: Why is 16 kHz the ASR standard sample rate, and how does it relate to Nyquist's theorem?
flashcards.a: By Nyquist, a sample rate f captures frequencies up to f/2. Speech-intelligibility-critical energy sits below ~8 kHz, so 16 kHz (8 kHz Nyquist limit) captures essentially all speech-relevant information without the extra cost of a higher rate.

flashcards.q: List the six steps of MFCC derivation in order.
flashcards.a: Framing (short overlapping windows) -> Windowing (Hamming, avoid spectral leakage) -> FFT (time to frequency domain) -> Mel filterbank (log-spaced triangular filters) -> Log (matches perceived loudness) -> DCT (decorrelates, keep first ~12-13 coefficients).

flashcards.q: Why does the mel scale use logarithmic spacing above ~1 kHz instead of linear Hz spacing?
flashcards.a: It mirrors human pitch perception: we discriminate pitch differences much more finely at low frequencies than high ones, so mel spacing allocates more filter resolution to the low-frequency range where speech carries the most phonetically distinctive information.

flashcards.q: What are the three independently-trained components Kaldi composes via WFST, and what specific pain killed this architecture?
flashcards.a: Acoustic model (audio->phoneme), pronunciation lexicon (word->phonemes), language model (word-sequence probability), composed via H∘C∘L∘G. Killed by: none of the three transfer between languages, so a new language needed real engineering-months of specialized, non-transferable work per language.

flashcards.q: What loss function does Wav2Vec2 use for fine-tuning, and what problem does it solve?
flashcards.a: CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) -- solves the lack of frame-level alignment between many audio frames and fewer target text tokens by summing probability over all valid alignments via a forward-backward dynamic-programming algorithm, using a blank token to distinguish repeated consecutive characters.

flashcards.q: What is the headline low-resource result from the Wav2Vec2 paper?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuning with just 10 minutes of labeled data, on top of pretraining on 53,000 hours of unlabeled audio (Libri-light), achieved 4.8/8.2 WER on clean/other test sets.

flashcards.q: How large is Whisper's training data, and what makes its supervision 'weak'?
flashcards.a: 680,000 hours of audio-transcript pairs scraped from the internet, spanning 96 languages -- weak because the transcripts are noisy web data, not carefully curated labels, unlike Wav2Vec2's small clean labeled fine-tuning set.

flashcards.q: Name Whisper's three characteristic failure modes and what architectural feature causes them.
flashcards.a: Hallucinated text on silence (generative decoder trained to always produce output), timestamp drift (independent 30-second chunk decoding compounds small errors across boundaries), repetition loops (autoregressive decoder stuck with no strong signal to advance) -- all rooted in the fixed 30-second processing window.

flashcards.q: Compare distil-whisper and whisper-large-v3-turbo on speed and accuracy tradeoff versus large-v3.
flashcards.a: distil-large-v3: 756M params (vs 1.54B), ~6x faster, within ~1% WER of full model. large-v3-turbo: 809M params (decoder pruned 32->4 layers), ~6-8x faster, only 0.3-0.7 percentage-point WER increase.

flashcards.q: Define WER precisely, and why is it a poor proxy for downstream task success?
flashcards.a: WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / (reference word count), via edit-distance alignment. Poor proxy because it weighs every word error equally -- a missed negation or wrong entity is one error with severe downstream impact, while a mis-transcribed filler word is one error with near-zero impact.

flashcards.q: What's the standard diarization pipeline, and what makes overlapping speech the hard problem?
flashcards.a: VAD isolates speech regions -> neural embedding model computes a speaker vector per segment -> clustering (commonly agglomerative) groups by similarity. Overlap is hard because classical architectures assign one speaker label per time segment, structurally wrong whenever two people talk simultaneously.

flashcards.q: What does pyannote 3.x's Powerset architecture do differently, and why should you check whether a DER comparison scores overlap?
flashcards.a: It treats overlapping-speaker combinations as their own output classes instead of one-label-per-frame. Old DER definitions often didn't score overlap at all, giving partial credit to systems that just picked the dominant speaker -- comparing an overlap-unaware DER to an overlap-aware one directly is apples-to-oranges.

flashcards.q: State the streaming-vs-batch ASR tradeoff in one sentence, and why Whisper isn't a native streaming model.
flashcards.a: More lookahead context improves accuracy but adds latency directly -- it's a single dial, not separable knobs. Whisper is architecturally batch-oriented (full attention over a fixed 30-second window); 'streaming Whisper' is a sliding-window workaround, not native incremental decoding.

flashcards.q: What's the standard efficient runtime for deploying any Whisper variant on GPU, and what does it use under the hood?
flashcards.a: faster-whisper (SYSTRAN), which reimplements Whisper inference using CTranslate2, a highly optimized C++ inference engine, independent of which specific model weights (large-v3, turbo, distil) you load.

flashcards.q: Give the deciding factor for choosing a managed transcription API vs self-hosting Whisper/faster-whisper.
flashcards.a: Volume and utilization: low/bursty volume favors a managed API's pay-per-use pricing over idle GPU cost; sustained high volume, on-prem/compliance requirements, or need for domain fine-tuning favors self-hosting.
